foods.name: Banana
foods.tagline: Famous for potassium. The water gets you first.
overview: Raw banana is about 75% water and carries 358 mg of potassium per 100 g, which is how it became the poster fruit for the mineral. A medium one weighs about 118 g.
Scaled to a 70 kg person, the potassium limit is about 26.7 kg. Water gets there first at about 8.4 kg, roughly 71 bananas, which says more about bananas being wet than being dangerous.

facts.label: Botanically
facts.value: A berry (the fruit, not the plant)

foods.funFact: Bananas are very slightly radioactive because of potassium-40, which spawned the informal "banana equivalent dose" used to explain radiation exposure.

foods.form: raw, with skin, no core or seeds
foods.tagline: An apple a day, minus the seeds, minus the toxicologist.

foods.name: Orange
foods.tagline: Vitamin C royalty, but the vitamin would take tonnes. Water gets there first.
overview: A raw orange is about 87% water, with 53.2 mg of vitamin C and 181 mg of potassium per 100 g. One 131 g orange carries about 70 mg of vitamin C.
Water sets the limit at about 7.3 kg, or 55 oranges. Vitamin C alone would need about 1.6 tonnes. Citric acid (about 9.1 g/L in fresh juice) would take 23.1 kg.
foods.funFact: The colour orange was named after the fruit, not the other way round: English had no word for it until the fruit arrived.

foods.name: Lemon
foods.form: raw, peeled flesh and juice (no peel)
foods.tagline: The one fruit here where something other than water sets the limit.
overview: Peeled lemon is about 89% water, with 53 mg of vitamin C and 138 mg of potassium per 100 g. The sour is citric acid: about 48 g per litre in freshly squeezed juice (Penniston et al., 2008).
Citric acid sets the limit at about 4.4 kg, roughly 75 average lemons. Your mouth and stomach would lodge formal complaints well before the arithmetic got a turn.

facts.value: About 48 g per litre (Penniston et al., 2008)

foods.funFact: In a 2008 study, freshly squeezed lemon juice carried about 48 g of citric acid per litre, roughly five times as much as fresh orange juice (9.1 g/L).

foods.name: Strawberry
foods.tagline: Not technically a berry. Technically about 91% water.
overview: Raw strawberries are about 91% water, with 58.8 mg of vitamin C and 153 mg of potassium per 100 g. A medium berry is only about 12 g, so the maths needs a lot of strawberries.
Water sets the limit at about 6.9 kg, or roughly 580 medium strawberries. You would run out of punnets, and then patience, before the toxicology got started.

facts.value: Not a true berry (an aggregate accessory fruit)

foods.funFact: The "seeds" on a strawberry are actually tiny separate fruits (achenes) sitting on the outside of the berry.

foods.name: Blueberry
foods.tagline: Small, blue, 84% water. Count your way up to thousands.
overview: Raw blueberries are about 84% water, with 77 mg of potassium and only 9.7 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, plus roughly 10 g of sugars, split between glucose and fructose. A cup is about 148 g.
Water sets the limit at about 7.5 kg, which is 51 cups of blueberries. At about 1.4 g a berry, you would be counting in thousands.
foods.funFact: The dusty white coating on a blueberry is a natural wax called bloom, made by the fruit itself, and it is a sign of freshness rather than a residue.

foods.form: raw, red or green seedless (European type)

foods.name: Kiwifruit

foods.funFact: Exporters Turners & Growers began calling it "kiwifruit" in 1959 instead of "Chinese gooseberry". The name nods to the nickname for New Zealanders, not (as is often claimed) the bird.

problems: USDA FoodData Central API (DEMO_KEY) rate-limited after about a dozen calls, so all composition values were read from the bulk SR Legacy CSV download (April 2018 release), whose URL is the compositionSource URL; each id is the fdcId, which can be looked up at fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-details/<id>/nutrients. Individual food-details pages were not opened. SR Legacy is not updated any more, so values are the last published SR figures.

Water LD50 is ">90 mL/kg" (no LD50 reached; ChemIDplus via PubChem, Food Research 21:348, 1956), a lower bound, treated as 90,000 mg/kg (matching substances.ts) at 1 mL = 1 g. HSDB lists no rat oral value for water (mouse ip only). Because it is a ">" figure, every water-limited headline is a floor, not a measured LD50, so confidence is "medium" for those foods.

Fructose dropped: neither HSDB nor ChemIDplus (via PubChem) lists an oral rat or mouse LD50 for fructose (only rabbit IV 15 g/kg), and no supplier SDS could be fetched (web search was unavailable and the Wayback copies were rate-limited). Fructose-rich fruits are modelled on glucose/sucrose only; none are limited by sugar anyway.

Potassium chloride rat oral 2600 mg/kg is cited from ChemIDplus via PubChem (Marhold, Czechoslovakia) and also appears in the INCHEM poison information monograph PIM 430 (Saxena, 1989), which I opened (its URL was not recorded, so it is not listed as a source link). HSDB lists mouse oral 383 mg/kg and guinea pig 2500 mg/kg; mouse values were not used because a rat value exists. If 383 mg/kg were used, potassium-limited numbers would shrink about 7x but would still be far larger than the water limits.

LD50 verification status: at the final check I re-confirmed the rat oral values for NaCl (3000), sucrose (29,700), glucose (25,800), ascorbic acid (11,900) and citric acid (3000 / 6730 / 11,700 / 12,000) against PubChem HSDB data, plus KCl mouse 383 / guinea pig 2500, and KCl rat 2600 via INCHEM PIM 430. I could NOT re-confirm the water figure (rat oral ">90 mL/kg"): PubChem serves the ChemIDplus acute-toxicity table through a script-loaded endpoint that would not return on recheck, so that value rests on a read earlier in the session. PubChem HSDB for water lists only mouse intraperitoneal values. Water drives 18 of the 20 headlines, so it is the first figure to re-verify.

Fun facts and botanical notes: Nix v. Hedden (1893, tomato as a vegetable for customs) and the 1959 kiwifruit naming (nickname for New Zealanders, not the bird) were checked against Wikipedia this session. The others (bromelain, bloom on blueberries, achenes, Anacardiaceae, Rosaceae, cantaloupe/Cantalupo, grenade/pomegranate, avocados ripening off the tree, nectarines, the PNAS 2019 grape plasma paper, oleuropein) are general knowledge that I could not source-check because web search was unavailable. They carry no figures except the PNAS year, so are worth a quick look before publishing.

Citric acid composition is not in USDA SR Legacy, so lemon and orange use Penniston et al. 2008 (J Endourol; Table 1, ion chromatography of squeezed juice, n=2 each: lemon 48.0 g/L, orange 9.10 g/L) as a proxy for the peeled flesh, with 1 mL = 1 g. Lemon is the only fruit where this makes citric acid the headline, so its confidence note flags the extra uncertainty.

Orange, lemon, pomegranate and the olives have no sucrose/glucose/fructose split in SR Legacy, so sugars are not modelled for them. At 8 to 15 g of sugar per 100 g, sugar limits would be tens of kilos regardless.

Trace minerals (iron, zinc, copper, manganese, magnesium, calcium, fluoride, selenium) and carotenoids were not assessed: no rat oral LD50 was looked up for them and at fruit-level amounts they are not plausible limiters. Fat in avocado and olives is shown as a fact only; no fat LD50 is used.

Olives: used USDA "Olives, pickled, canned or bottled, green" (sodium 1,556 mg/100 g). Ripe canned (black) olives in SR Legacy have 735 mg sodium/100 g, which would give roughly twice the lethal mass. Brine strength varies a lot by brand, so the headline (about 5.3 kg) is close to the 5 kg "absurd" cut-off; even a much saltier jar would still be "large" and far past any real serving.
No fixed LD50 has been sourced for persin (avocado), bromelain (pineapple) or other food-specific compounds; none are modelled.

Emoji: no raspberry or pomegranate emoji exists, so raspberry uses the strawberry emoji (🍓) and pomegranate uses 🔴. Unit "10 olives (27 g)" is derived as 10 x USDA 2.7 g per olive; "half cup of arils" is USDA 87 g for 0.5 cup. Orange lists USDA "fruit (2-5/8 in dia)" at 131 g as the typical orange.

Pears use the generic USDA "Pears, raw" entry; apple uses "Apples, raw, with skin"; grapes use "Grapes, red or green (European type, such as Thompson seedless), raw". Pomegranate USDA data is for the edible arils including their seeds.

The tomato is in the fruit category per the brief; it is the wettest of the 20 (94.5% water). All 20 land in foods; none flagged as plausible by the maths. Flagged items are the three cyanogenic seed/stone cases (apple seeds, cherry and peach stones), which are not in the food entries themselves.
